title: Hard questions are allowed
hook: A doubt doesn't mean you made a mistake. It means you're thinking.

screens.text: Maybe you read something online that bothered you. Maybe a question keeps coming back at night. Doubts are normal, they're allowed, and there's a good way to handle them.
**You're not the only one.** In a 2025 survey of 618 American converts, about 1 in 4 said doubts had made them think about leaving Islam [Yaqeen 2025].

screens.prompt: In that survey, what was the biggest doubt topic?

options.feedback: Yes, 44%. Next came feeling the rules limit freedom (37%). Fewer (21%) doubted God exists. Most doubts are about the rules, not God.
Not quite. That was 21%. Rules about men and women (44%) and freedom (37%) came first. Most doubts are about the rules.
Close: that was second, at 37%. Rules about men and women came first (44%). Only 21% doubted God exists.

screens.text: **Even the Companions had them.** Some told the Prophet ﷺ they had thoughts too awful to say out loud. He didn't scold them. He said being troubled by those thoughts was a sign of real faith [Muslim 132].
bubbles: And the prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) asked Allah to show him how He brings the dead to life. He already believed. He asked so his heart could be at rest [Q 2:260].

screens.title: What a doubt is, and isn't

cards.front: "If I have a doubt, maybe I'm not really Muslim."
cards.back: A question isn't a rejection. Feeling unsure is not leaving Islam. Leaving is a choice to reject it.

cards.front: "Good Muslims never wonder about this stuff."
cards.back: The Companions did, and told the Prophet ﷺ. Their worry about it was itself a sign of faith.

cards.front: "I should keep my questions to myself."
cards.back: Hidden questions tend to grow. Asked questions usually shrink. Scholars have worked on these same questions for centuries.
Some take time and study. "I don't know yet, let me find out" is an honest, grown-up answer.

screens.text: **Two different things can feel like doubt:** an honest question, and a whisper.
bubbles: An **honest question**: you want to understand. Write it down, then ask someone trustworthy.
A **whisper** (*waswasa*): a looping thought, like "But who created God?", that brings anxiety, not answers.
The Prophet ﷺ said that when a whisper comes, seek refuge in Allah and stop following it [Bukhari 3276]. Say *A'udhu billah* and turn to something else.

items.why: Curious and calm: that's a question. Bring it to a trusted teacher.

items.why: That's a whisper. Say A'udhu billah and turn to something else.

screens.situation: Hannah reads a viral post claiming the Qur'an hates women. Her stomach drops. It's late, and she's alone with her phone.

options.text: Write the question down, sleep, then ask her mentor or the AI guide for the verse's context and a trusted answer
options.feedback: Yes. The panic fades by morning. The question stays and gets a real answer from someone qualified.
Not quite. Keep praying while you search. Prayer is the place to ask Allah for clarity.

options.text: Push it down and never think about it again
options.feedback: Not quite. Ignored questions usually come back louder. It's better to ask it calmly.

options.text: Argue with the person in the comments
options.feedback: Not quite. Comment sections rarely give answers, and arguing at midnight won't settle her heart.

steps.text: Separate the question from the panic. Write it down.
Go to trusted teachers, not comment sections.
Keep praying while you look. Bring the question into your du'a: "Allah, show me what's true." He hears [Q 2:186].
Re-read why you said yes to Islam (your Day 1 reflection).
If the doubts come with constant anxiety or dark thoughts, tell someone. That deserves care too.

screens.text: Drag along the line. A dip isn't the end of the story.

points.label: A question hits
points.text: Something you read won't leave you alone. Feeling unsure is not leaving Islam.

points.label: Written down
points.text: The panic is separate from the question now. It can wait until morning.

points.label: Asked, still praying
points.text: A trusted teacher, your mentor, your du'a. Asked questions usually shrink.

points.label: Heart at rest
points.text: Like Ibrahim, you can believe and still ask, so your heart can be at rest [Q 2:260].

screens.prompt: Is there a question on your mind right now? Write it down, as honestly as you like. You don't have to answer it today. You can share it with your mentor if you want to talk it through.

screens.text: Do something with one question you've been carrying.
steps: Or send it to your imam with "Ask my imam" (it can be anonymous)
screens.optional_extra: If nothing's bothering you right now, save today's steps for when something does.

screens.text: Doubts are normal. Write the question down, ask someone trustworthy, and keep praying while you look.
Asking is part of believing. You're in good company.

check.prompt: Does having a doubt mean you've left Islam?

options.text: No. A question isn't a rejection; leaving is choosing to reject Islam
options.feedback: Right. Even the Companions had troubling thoughts, and the Prophet ﷺ called their worry a sign of faith.

options.text: Yes, a real Muslim never doubts
options.feedback: Not quite. Doubts are common. What matters is what you do with them.

check.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ advise for looping "who created God?" whispers?

options.text: Seek refuge in Allah and stop following the thought
options.feedback: Right. Say A'udhu billah and turn to something else. Honest questions are different: ask those.

options.text: Debate it in your head until you win
options.feedback: Not quite. Whispers feed on attention. Seek refuge in Allah and move on.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Yaqeen Institute's 2025 *Becoming Muslim* survey (n=618 US converts): 23% said doubts made them consider leaving; the top doubt topics were gender rules (44%) and rules restricting freedom (37%); God's existence was 21% [Yaqeen 2025; T1 Fact-Check Log #28]. The sample only includes people who still identify as Muslim.
- Companions felt thoughts too grave to say; the Prophet ﷺ said their distress over them was clear faith [Muslim 132].
- Ibrahim asked to see how Allah gives life to the dead "so my heart may be satisfied," while already believing [Q 2:260].
- For intrusive "who created your Lord?" whispers: seek refuge in Allah and stop [Bukhari 3276]. This is for looping whispers, not honest questions.
- Feeling unsure is not leaving Islam; leaving is a choice to reject it (scholar question Q20).

**Likely questions** (follow Spec §6.2 rule 5: take doubts seriously, never shame, never pressure, never argue anyone into belief; offer a mentor or scholar)
- *"Why are there different rules for men and women?"* Acknowledge it's the most common convert question. Give the mainstream picture briefly: equal in worth and reward before Allah; some roles and rulings differ; much of what people see is culture, not Islam. Offer Day 75 and a female mentor or imam for depth. Don't dismiss the feeling.
- *"Doesn't Islam take away my freedom?"* Listen first. Islam's limits are few and most things are allowed (Day 49); faith is chosen freely [Q 2:256]. Ask which rule feels heaviest; route specifics to the imam.
- *"How do Muslims know God exists?"* Short: reason (things that begin need a cause), the order and beauty of the world, the Qur'an, and personal experience. Offer to go deeper or connect them with a teacher.
- *"I have a doubt I'm scared to say."* Thank them for trusting you. Reassure that saying it isn't a sin and doesn't make them a non-Muslim. Let them say it, then answer gently or route it.
- *"I think I want to leave."* Don't panic, argue or threaten. Ask what's going on; separate struggling from denying; offer a human (mentor, imam, or a trusted scholar) and say they're welcome either way to talk. Never mention punishments.

**Escalate:** questions about the punishment for apostasy (fixed policy, rule 11: short calm mainstream answer, then the imam); specific verses or hadith the guide can't answer from approved sources; any convert who says they want to leave Islam (offer a mentor or imam conversation, with consent). **Safety:** if doubt comes with hopelessness, self-harm thoughts or crisis, follow rule 6 immediately.

**Don't**
- Don't shame, threaten, mention Hell, or say "doubting is a sin."
- Don't overwhelm with arguments or link-dump. One clear point, then offer more.
- Don't claim certainty you don't have; say "I'm not sure, let's ask the imam."
- Don't diagnose. If doubts look like scrupulosity or anxiety, gently suggest talking to someone, and Day 45.
